chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ali, from Amr ibn Saeed, from Musaddaq ibn Sadaqa, from Ammar ibn Musa, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

He was asked about the meal-table when wine or an intoxicant is drunk upon it, so he (peace be upon him) said: 'The meal-table is prohibited.' And he (peace be upon him) was asked: 'If a man stands by a set-up meal-table, eating from what is on it, and with the man is an intoxicant, and he did not give it to anyone who is on it to drink afterwards,' so he (peace be upon him) said: 'It is not prohibited until it is drunk upon it. And if it is placed after it is drunk, [then] the Falouzaj [a sweet drink], so eat it, for it is another meal-table,' meaning: eat the Falouzaj.
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a meal table if wine is drunk on it?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) establishes that a dining table becomes ritually impure (najis) for consumption only when wine or an intoxicant is actually drunk upon it, distinguishing this from mere presence. He further clarifies that if a new food item like Falouzaj is placed after the intoxicant is consumed, it is considered a separate entity and remains permissible, illustrating the Shia juristic principle of distinguishing between the contaminating agent and the contaminated surface based on actual usage. This ruling underscores the practical application of 'transfer of impurity' (intiqal al-najāsah) in daily life, ensuring that mere proximity to intoxicants does not render all associated food haram.
